axes.label: Soteriology
axes.description: Whether salvation is God's work alone or involves genuine human cooperation.

axes.label: Baptism
axes.description: Whether baptism is for professing believers only or also for their infant children.

axes.label: Spiritual Gifts
axes.description: Whether miraculous gifts like tongues and prophecy ceased with the apostles or continue today.

axes.label: Eschatology
axes.description: Whether Christ returns before a future earthly millennium or reigns now from heaven.

axes.label: Covenant and Dispensations
axes.description: Whether God works through distinct eras and peoples or one unfolding covenant of grace.

axes.label: Scripture
axes.description: Whether the Bible is without error in all it affirms or authoritative without strict errorlessness.

axes.label: Worship
axes.description: Whether worship must be explicitly commanded in Scripture or may include anything not forbidden.

axes.label: Church Government
axes.description: Whether each local church governs itself or stands under wider church authority.

axes.label: Gender Roles
axes.description: Whether Scripture reserves certain offices and roles by gender or opens all ministry to women.

axes.label: Faith and Assurance
axes.description: Whether saving faith necessarily transforms the life or rests on belief alone.

axes.label: Baptism and Communion
axes.description: Whether the ordinances are symbols of grace already received or means by which grace is given.

axes.label: Sanctification
axes.description: Whether a crisis experience of full cleansing is possible or holiness grows only gradually.

traditions.name: Reformed / Calvinist
traditions.description: Confesses God's sovereign grace in salvation: unconditional election, definite atonement, and perseverance of the saints. Worships by the regulative principle, baptizes believers' children, and reads the Bible through covenant theology. Includes Presbyterians and Reformed Baptists.

traditions.name: Confessional Lutheran
traditions.description: Centers on justification by faith alone and the real presence of Christ in Word and sacrament. Holds monergistic conversion with universal atonement, baptizes infants, and follows historic liturgy under the Lutheran confessions. Law and gospel frame its reading of Scripture.

traditions.name: Wesleyan / Arminian
traditions.description: Teaches that God's prevenient grace frees every person to respond to the gospel, and that believers may fall from grace. Expects both gradual growth and crisis experiences of entire sanctification. Methodist and Holiness churches typically baptize infants and ordain women.

traditions.name: Confessional Baptist
traditions.description: Calvinistic in soteriology but baptistic in ecclesiology: believers' baptism by immersion, congregational government, and usually a memorialist Lord's Supper. Affirms the 1689 London Baptist Confession alongside strict biblical inerrancy.

traditions.name: Pentecostal / Charismatic
traditions.description: Expects the miraculous gifts of the Spirit — tongues, prophecy, healing — to operate today, often with a distinct baptism in the Holy Spirit after conversion. Typically Arminian, credobaptist, premillennial, and expressive in worship.

traditions.name: Anabaptist
traditions.description: Baptizes only confessing believers into a disciplined, discipleship-shaped community. Emphasizes the Sermon on the Mount, simple worship, congregational discernment, and a costly obedience that proves faith genuine.

traditions.name: Anglican
traditions.description: Worships through the Book of Common Prayer with bishops, infant baptism, and a sacramental view of communion. Theologically broad — from Reformed to Anglo-Catholic — but classically holds Scripture, tradition, and reason together.

traditions.name: Dispensationalist
traditions.description: Reads the Bible through distinct dispensations, keeps Israel and the church as separate peoples with separate destinies, and expects a pretribulational rapture and literal millennium. Usually credobaptist, memorialist, inerrantist, and 'free grace' on assurance.

theologians.name: John Calvin
theologians.blurb: Genevan Reformer whose Institutes systematized the doctrines of grace.

theologians.name: Martin Luther
theologians.blurb: German Reformer who recovered justification by faith alone.

theologians.name: John Wesley
theologians.blurb: Founder of Methodism; preached prevenient grace and entire sanctification.

theologians.name: Jonathan Edwards
theologians.blurb: American theologian of revival, divine sovereignty, and religious affections.

theologians.name: Charles Spurgeon
theologians.blurb: Calvinistic Baptist 'Prince of Preachers' in Victorian London.

theologians.name: C.S. Lewis
theologians.blurb: Oxford apologist whose Mere Christianity shaped lay evangelical faith.

theologians.name: Karl Barth
theologians.blurb: Swiss theologian whose neo-orthodox theology of the Word reshaped 20th-century Protestant thought.

theologians.name: N.T. Wright
theologians.blurb: New Testament scholar behind the New Perspective on Paul.

theologians.name: John Piper
theologians.blurb: Reformed Baptist pastor who taught Christian hedonism: God glorified in our joy in him.

theologians.name: R.C. Sproul
theologians.blurb: Presbyterian teacher who popularized Reformed theology through Ligonier Ministries.

theologians.name: Menno Simons
theologians.blurb: Dutch Anabaptist leader who gave his name to the Mennonites.

theologians.name: D.L. Moody
theologians.blurb: American evangelist whose premillennial crusades shaped popular evangelicalism.

theologians.name: A.W. Tozer
theologians.blurb: Alliance pastor whose deeper-life writings on the Holy Spirit shaped charismatic evangelicalism.

theologians.name: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
theologians.blurb: German Lutheran pastor-theologian, martyred for resisting the Nazis; wrote on discipleship and costly grace.

theologians.name: J.I. Packer
theologians.blurb: Anglican evangelical whose Knowing God taught a generation to think biblically about God.

questions.text: If science and the Bible seem to disagree, I trust the Bible.
I believe every part of the Bible is true, not just the spiritual parts.
I love when churches try creative new things in worship.
I'd feel uneasy if my church added something to worship just because it's creative.
I like the idea that each church answers to no one but God.
Churches are healthier when they're accountable to leaders beyond their own walls.
Getting baptized felt — or would feel — most meaningful as my own personal decision.
Baptism doesn't really count until someone is old enough to choose it themselves.
I love the idea of babies being welcomed into the faith through baptism.
Communion is mainly about remembering what Jesus did.
I feel like I actually meet God in a special way during communion.
Baptism is mostly a public way of showing you're a Christian.
I expect God still does miracles like healing and prophecy today.
Speaking in tongues is something I'd be open to in my own prayer life.
I believe God still gives people specific words for others today.
I'd have a hard time seeing a woman as my senior pastor.
I'd be totally comfortable with a woman preaching every Sunday.
When I read the Bible, it feels like one continuous story about Jesus.
The Old Testament feels like a different era when God worked by different rules.
I think of Israel and the church as two different groups in God's plan.
I believe God still has special plans for the Jewish people.
I think Jesus will return and set up a real kingdom on earth.
I think Jesus is already reigning now — the end is more about him wrapping things up.
If someone's life never changes, I doubt their faith was real.
I know Christians whose lives look messy but whose faith I don't question.
I feel secure that God will keep hold of me even in my worst seasons.
I'll be fighting against sin for the rest of my life.
I believe it's possible to reach a point where sin doesn't control you anymore.
No one would ever choose God on their own — he has to change their heart first.
God wants everyone to be saved, and it's up to each person to accept or reject him.
Christ's death made salvation possible for all people, but it becomes effective only for those who believe.
God's grace enables every person to respond to the gospel, but each person must freely choose to believe.
God's choice of who to save was based on his foreknowledge of who would freely believe.
The Bible's authority rests on its saving message, not on being error-free in historical or scientific details.
Some parts of the Bible reflect the limited scientific understanding of their time.
When the Bible's human authors wrote, God guided their words so fully that the result is exactly what he intended.
Baptism is the New Testament counterpart to circumcision, marking out believers' children as part of God's covenant people.
Someone baptized as an infant should be baptized again after coming to personal faith.
The office of apostle, with authority to speak new revelation, no longer exists.
Speaking in tongues is the expected initial sign of being baptized in the Holy Spirit.
Christians should actively seek and practice spiritual gifts like healing and prophecy.
Christians will be taken up to heaven (the rapture) before a coming seven-year tribulation.
The church is the continuation and fulfillment of Israel in God's plan.
Jesus could return at any moment, without any prophesied events needing to happen first.
The Old Testament law no longer binds Christians directly; we live entirely under grace.
God's moral law, like the Ten Commandments, still guides Christian obedience today.
The church began at Pentecost as something entirely new, not as the continuation of Israel.
Drama, dance, and visual arts have a proper place in Sunday worship.
It is wrong to introduce worship elements just because they attract visitors.
The final human authority in a local church is the congregation as a whole.
Pastors should be appointed by church leaders, not chosen by congregational vote.
God uses baptism to actually convey grace and forgiveness to the recipient.
Christ is spiritually present in the Lord's Supper in a special way, beyond his general presence everywhere.
The Lord's Supper should be celebrated frequently — weekly if possible.
Growth in holiness happens gradually over a lifetime, not in a single crisis moment.
A Christian can reach a state of not sinning willfully in this life.
Husbands have a God-given leadership role in the home.
Men and women are equally called to all forms of ministry; gifts, not gender, determine roles.
If someone claims to be a Christian but lives in unrepentant sin, we should doubt whether their faith is real.
Repentance from sin is part of what it means to believe the gospel, not an optional add-on.
God's decree to save the elect logically preceded his decree to permit the fall.
Regeneration (the new birth) happens before and causes a person's faith, not the other way around.
The Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978) accurately expresses what Christians should believe about the Bible.
The Bible's authority comes from the God who speaks through it, not from a theory about how it was written.
The children of believers should receive communion as well as baptism.
The 'perfect' of 1 Corinthians 13 refers to the completion of the New Testament canon.
The great tribulation already happened when Rome destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70.
The world will grow progressively more Christianized before Christ returns.
The 'covenant of works' with Adam and the 'covenant of grace' in Christ are the right framework for reading the whole Bible.
Only psalms should be sung in gathered worship; uninspired hymns are not permitted.
An unbroken line of bishops back to the apostles matters for a church's legitimacy.
In communion, Christ's body and blood are truly present 'in, with, and under' the bread and wine.
John Wesley's doctrine of entire sanctification is a faithful reading of Scripture.
The Bible's instructions about women remaining silent in church apply to all times and cultures.
Jesus must be received as Lord, not just as Savior, for salvation.
God's grace in salvation cannot be resisted by those he intends to save.
God has eternally decreed everything that happens, including who is saved and who is lost.
A true Christian can, through persistent unbelief, finally lose their salvation.
The Holy Spirit's convicting work can be resisted and rejected by the sinner.
Apparent contradictions in the Bible can always be resolved with enough study.
Jesus's own view of the Old Testament commits Christians to affirming its complete truthfulness.
God accommodated his revelation to the cultural and scientific assumptions of the original audience.
The mode of baptism doesn't matter — immersion, pouring, and sprinkling are all valid when done in the triune name.
Delaying baptism until a child is old enough to give a mature profession of faith is the wisest practice.
The baptism in the Holy Spirit is a distinct experience after conversion.
Christians today should expect God to heal the sick in response to prayer.
Current events in the Middle East are fulfilling biblical prophecy about the end times.
Prophecies given to Israel should be read literally as referring to ethnic Israel, not spiritually as referring to the church.
The New Testament authors sometimes draw out a deeper meaning from Old Testament texts than the original author consciously intended.
A church's worship style should adapt to its local culture to reach people effectively.
Worship should engage the emotions, not just the mind.
A worship service should center on preaching, prayer, and the ordinances rather than on creating an emotional experience.
A single pastor, rather than a team of elders, should lead each congregation.
Local churches should cooperate in associations or conventions while remaining self-governing.
Baptism replaces circumcision as the sign of belonging to God's covenant people.
Baptism is necessary for salvation.
Even the most mature Christians remain sinners who need daily repentance.
The normal Christian life includes real victory over deliberate sin, not just forgiveness for it.
The baptism in the Holy Spirit empowers believers for holy living and witness.
Complementarianism best honors both the equality and the differences God built into men and women.
Restricting church offices by gender has more to do with culture than with Scripture.
Assurance of salvation comes from trusting God's promise, not from examining your own obedience.
The 'free grace' teaching associated with Dallas Seminary faithfully represents the gospel.
Saving faith includes a commitment to obey Christ, even before a person understands all that obedience requires.
Once a person has believed, their eternal destiny is secure even if they later abandon the faith.
